content: Developing a standardized training curriculum for fistula management would promote its widespread adoption and enhance its overall impact. By including recommendations for standardized postoperative care, the capacity of fistula treatment centers to deliver high-quality services to women affected by obstetric urinary fistula would be significantly strengthened. The implementation and impact of the recommendations outlined in this guideline should be monitored at health service, regional, and national levels. Key indicators for evaluation include the rate of fistula repair breakdown before and after hospital discharge, the prevalence of urinary incontinence post-discharge, the duration of hospital stays, and maternal satisfaction with the care provided. These indicators can be adapted regionally and nationally to assess adherence to and the effectiveness of the recommendations. In collaboration with the monitoring and evaluation teams of the WHO Departments of Reproductive Health and Research (RHR) and Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health (MCA), data on the implementation of these recommendations at country and regional levels will be collected and analyzed in the short to medium term. This will help evaluate their influence on national policies across WHO Member States. The guideline will be updated five years after its publication, in line with the WHO’s GREAT Network approach, which systematically identifies and addresses evidence gaps following guideline implementation. However, if significant new evidence emerges earlier, the guideline will be revised accordingly. The WHO Steering Group will continue to monitor research developments in the field of obstetric fistula. Any concerns regarding the validity of the recommendations will be promptly communicated to global implementers, and plans for updates will be initiated as needed. As the guideline approaches the end of its five-year validity period, a technical officer or designated WHO staff member, in collaboration with the Steering Group, will review the recommendations in light of current evidence to determine the need for new guidance. If new evidence raises concerns about the validity of the recommendations, the systematic review addressing the primary question will be updated using the original search strategy to capture recent studies. Any new questions identified during the scoping exercise will undergo a similar process of evidence retrieval, synthesis, and grading, following WHO’s guideline development procedures. WHO also welcomes suggestions for additional questions to be included in future updates. The guideline development process involved contributions from a diverse group of experts, methodologists, and observers, ensuring a comprehensive and evidence-based approach. Conflicts of interest were managed appropriately, with some members participating without voting rights to maintain the integrity of the recommendations. The evidence-to-decision framework considered the quality of evidence, values, preferences, benefits, harms, cost implications, equity, acceptability, and feasibility to determine the strength and direction of the recommendations.
